slides.title: Bombykol triggers silkmoth mate searching
body: **Pheromones** are chemical signals exchanged between members of a species. Male silkmoths, _Bombyx mori_, respond to the female pheromone **bombykol** with a forward walking surge, alternating zigzag turns and wider looping search when further odor contacts are absent.

Shiota and colleagues measured body angle in tethered males and source finding during free walking. A single bombykol pulse elicited the complete searching sequence in both normal moths and moths lacking a pheromone-binding protein. Thus, the sequence could persist despite altered peripheral response kinetics.

At repeated stimulation rates of 0.83 and 2 Hz, mutants spent less time surging and more time turning. Detecting pheromone is therefore insufficient for efficient tracking: the sensory system must also distinguish successive encounters. These behavioral differences do not establish the identity of the central circuit generating each movement.

slides.title: Turbulence separates odor into intermittent strands
body: An **odor plume** is the distribution of odor-bearing air transported from a source. Atmospheric turbulence divides that distribution into brief encounters separated by clean-air gaps. Murlis, Willis and Cardé measured plume intermittency in an open field and a forest rather than assuming a smooth concentration gradient.

The investigators released negatively charged air ions as a tracer and recorded fluctuations at downwind detectors. Signals were present only about 20% of the time in both environments. Sampling extended to 20 m downwind in the field and 10 m in the forest.

These measurements establish a discontinuous physical input at the detector, not the activity of a silkmoth neuron. Ionized air approximates plume transport but is not chemically identical to pheromone. Responses to intermittent odor must therefore be interpreted in relation to both environmental structure and the sensory preparation.

slides.title: Forest plumes contain longer gaps between bursts
body: **Bursts** are groups of closely spaced tracer peaks separated by longer gaps. Murlis and colleagues compared their timing in field and forest recordings. Although signal occupancy was about 20% in both environments, equal occupancy did not imply equal patterns of odor availability.

Forest interburst gaps lasted at least three times longer than field gaps. A burst contained about seven tracer spikes in the forest and three in the field. The environment therefore changed the clustering of encounters, even when the fraction of time containing signal was similar.

Longer gaps can permit searching movements to develop before odor returns. That behavioral implication follows from combining plume measurements with separate moth experiments; the tracer study itself did not identify a motor program or measure silkmoth source-finding success. A single mean concentration cannot describe the temporal challenge imposed by these plumes.

slides.title: Antennal voltage is an imperfect odor readout
body: An **electroantennogram**, or EAG, measures the summed electrical response of an antenna to odor. Murlis and colleagues paired ion-tracer measurements with male gypsy-moth antennal responses to the pheromone disparlure. This biological comparison tested whether tracer intermittency resembled stimulation reaching an insect sensory organ.

The pheromone source was positioned about 10 cm from the ion source. Ion bursts became weaker with distance, whereas EAG burst strength did not decrease in the same systematic way. Antennal responses also depended on how quickly consecutive stimuli arrived.

EAG voltage is therefore not a simple linear measure of airborne pheromone concentration. Receptor sensitivity and recovery shape the recorded waveform. These gypsy-moth measurements validate aspects of plume encounter timing but cannot be assigned directly to silkmoth receptor neurons or interpreted as recordings of a central neural circuit.

slides.title: One odor strand evokes a short upwind surge
body: Vickers and Baker exposed flying male tobacco budworms, _Heliothis virescens_, to single strands of their species-specific six-component pheromone blend. After interrupting an established plume, they delivered an isolated filament and synchronized its passage with calibrated lights moving at wind speed.

The average upwind surge covered 13.4 cm and lasted 0.38 s. Its onset followed odor contact by about 0.30 s. Males cast across the wind before and after the surge; no-filament control trials produced no upwind displacement by casting males.

A brief sensory event can therefore trigger a motor response that outlasts the event. The measurement concerns flying tobacco budworms, not walking silkmoths, and its numerical latency must not be transferred between species. The experiment establishes the timing of behavior without identifying the neurons maintaining the response.

slides.title: Frequent contacts sustain straighter upwind flight
body: Vickers and Baker varied pheromone delivery from 1 to 10 filaments/s while holding wind speed at 0.6 m/s. Each pulse lasted 20 ms, and air flow through the delivery device remained 5 mL/s. Flight trajectories were recorded from below the wind tunnel.

Fewer than 4 filaments/s activated males and elicited casting but did not sustain upwind flight. At 4 filaments/s, upwind trajectories remained tortuous. At 10 filaments/s, flight was straighter and contained less crosswind casting; 5 filaments/s produced an intermediate pattern.

Repeated encounters can renew forward responses before casting fully develops. Constant wind speed excludes wind-velocity changes as the explanation, although changing pulse rate also changes odor delivery through time. The experiment does not isolate every integrated-dose variable or establish an identical frequency threshold in Bombyx mori.

slides.title: Casting follows the loss of detectable odor
body: Vickers and Baker recorded local pheromone encounters during free flight using an excised third antenna mounted on a male’s thorax. Both of the animal’s own antennae remained intact. The mounted antenna supplied an EAG while synchronized video recorded the carrier’s trajectory.

Casting began on average 0.30 s after the last recorded filament contact. Relatively steady upwind flight involved more frequent encounters than crosswind flight. The video and EAG records were synchronized within 0.01 s, allowing behavioral timing to be compared with local sensory exposure.

Loss of intermittent input can release a different search movement without requiring the moth to detect a spatial concentration gradient. The mounted antenna sampled odor near the head but did not measure spikes in the animal’s brain. Correlated contact and movement cannot identify a specific inhibitory or excitatory central synapse.

slides.title: A trackball separates odor, wind and visual inputs
body: Yamada and colleagues studied walking male Bombyx mori using a **virtual reality** preparation: movement on a trackball updated the animal’s position in a controlled odor field. Odor ports could stimulate the two antennae independently, while wind arrived from four directions.

Visual stimulation supplied **optic flow**, the movement of a visual scene associated with self-motion. Odor, wind and visual conditions could be combined or reversed independently. A search was successful when the virtual position entered a 10-mm radius around the source within 300 s.

This preparation separates sensory influences that normally covary during walking. The authors compared performance with free-walking experiments, but a tethered virtual search still differs from unrestricted movement toward a real female. The experiment measures multisensory behavior rather than directly identifying the synapses that combine those cues.

slides.title: Wind information steers walking toward the source
body: In the virtual-reality study, males received odor alone, odor plus wind, or odor plus visual motion. Additional treatments reversed wind or visual direction while keeping the other available information controlled. These interventions tested the contribution of cue direction rather than simply increasing stimulation.

Correctly aligned wind improved source-finding success relative to odor alone. Reversed wind reduced success and increased downwind headings. Visual motion without wind produced trajectories more similar to odor-only search than did the addition of wind.

**Anemotaxis** is orientation relative to wind. The results support a role for wind direction in silkmoth odor-guided walking, while visual effects depend on the sensory context. They do not establish that odor concentration itself supplies direction or that the animal uses one fixed search rule in every cue combination.

slides.title: Bombykol detection begins in antennal sensory hairs
body: **Olfactory receptor neurons**, or ORNs, are sensory cells that convert odor exposure into electrical activity. In male Bombyx mori, long **sensilla trichodea**, hairlike structures on the antenna, house paired pheromone-responsive neurons. Their sensory endings contact the fluid inside each sensillum.

Sakurai and colleagues used receptor-gene expression, fluorescent labeling and in situ hybridization to identify the bombykol-responsive population. **BmOR1** is the ligand-selective receptor expressed by these neurons; the neighboring bombykal-responsive neuron expresses BmOR3. Bombykal is the corresponding aldehyde rather than the alcohol bombykol.

The separate receptor populations distinguish chemical channels before central processing. Expression and localization establish cell identity but do not by themselves measure ion flow or explain the behavioral meaning assigned to each channel. Those functions require electrophysiological and behavioral tests of the identified sensory population.

slides.title: Distinct receptor neurons resolve pheromone identity
body: A **single-sensillum recording** measures spikes near the sensory neurons housed in one antennal hair. Sakurai and colleagues distinguished the large-amplitude spikes of the bombykol neuron from the smaller spikes of the bombykal neuron while presenting chemically different ligands.

Control males responded through the bombykol channel to bombykol but not to the diamondback-moth ligand Z11-16:Ald. Introducing its receptor, PxOR1, into BmOR1-expressing neurons added responses to that aldehyde while retaining the original bombykol response.

The manipulation changed which chemical could excite an existing sensory channel. It did not convert the neighboring bombykal neuron or establish that all antennal hairs respond identically. Spike amplitude separates recorded units in this preparation; amplitude alone is not a universal molecular signature of a receptor.

slides.title: A foreign receptor adds a new sensory response
body: Sakurai and colleagues used the **GAL4/UAS system**, a genetic driver-and-target arrangement, to express PxOR1 in Bombyx bombykol-responsive neurons. PxOR1 was added alongside the native receptor rather than replacing or deleting BmOR1. Males bearing only one genetic component served as controls.

The manipulated neurons gained responses to Z11-16:Ald but not the corresponding tested acetate and alcohol compounds. Dose-response recordings retained responsiveness to bombykol. The added receptor’s transcript abundance was approximately ten times lower than that of native BmOR1.

Chemical selectivity can therefore change without changing the identity of the sensory pathway. Lower expression may contribute to differing response thresholds, but transcript abundance is not a direct count of functioning channels at the membrane. The experiment does not establish that receptor proteins themselves encode the motor sequence.

slides.title: Receptor addition changes mate-search initiation
body: Sakurai and colleagues tested whether the newly detected aldehyde could activate behavior through the bombykol pathway. Transgenic males expressing PxOR1 in BmOR1 neurons initiated wing flapping and pheromone-search walking in response to Z11-16:Ald. Parental genetic controls did not acquire that response.

Walking trajectories after the new ligand included the characteristic searching sequence. The manipulated males also attempted copulation with diamondback-moth females while retaining responsiveness to bombykol. Chemical recognition was altered without replacing the male’s existing central sensory-to-motor pathway.

The behavioral result connects receptor-neuron activation to initiation of a species-typical program. It does not imply that the foreign receptor contains a walking algorithm or that every aspect of successful reproduction was transferred. The central interpretation depends on the identity of the activated channel as well as the molecule detected.

slides.title: Receptor addition preserves central axon targets
body: A **glomerulus** is a region of concentrated sensory terminals and their interacting central neurons. The male silkmoth **macroglomerular complex**, or MGC, contains enlarged pheromone-processing glomeruli. BmOR1 sensory axons terminate in the **toroid**, a glomerulus dedicated to bombykol input.

Sakurai and colleagues compared fluorescently labeled axon terminals before and after PxOR1 addition. Axons carrying the modified chemical response still innervated the toroid rather than shifting to the neighboring cumulus. The new ligand therefore entered an existing central channel.

Preserved targeting supports an interpretation in which a changed peripheral detector gains access to established behavioral wiring. It does not prove that every synaptic weight or developmental property remained unchanged. Gross anatomical targeting and functional output are complementary evidence, rather than a complete synapse-by-synapse reconstruction.

slides.title: Bombykol receptors require a second subunit
body: The functional bombykol receptor combines the ligand-selective subunit BmOR1 with **Orco**, a broadly conserved olfactory co-receptor. A **heteromeric** complex contains different protein subunits. The older silkmoth name BmOr2 refers to this co-receptor rather than a second bombykol-selective detector.

Sato and colleagues expressed insect receptor pairs in non-insect cells and measured odor-evoked electrical currents. Nakagawa and colleagues then examined the Bombyx pair in frog oocytes using controlled voltage and amino-acid substitutions. Both preparations separate receptor function from an intact moth brain.

The evidence supports a ligand-gated, nonselective cation conductance associated with the receptor complex. **Cations** are positively charged ions; their movement can change membrane voltage. slides.title: Receptor residues alter cation selectivity
body: **Ion selectivity** describes the relative ease with which different ions pass through a channel. Nakagawa and colleagues changed conserved amino acids in the Bombyx BmOR1–Orco complex and recorded bombykol-evoked currents from frog oocytes. Each test changed one subunit while retaining the other in its normal form.

Replacing extracellular sodium with potassium allowed comparison of **reversal potentials**, the voltage at which net current changes direction. BmOR1 D299N and E356Q reduced relative potassium permeability; Orco Y464A increased it. Thus, substitutions in either protein could affect the ions carried by the complex.

slides.title: Chemical modification probes receptor function
body: Nakagawa and colleagues replaced selected receptor residues with **cysteine**, an amino acid whose exposed chemical group can react with a modifying reagent. slides.title: A binding protein shapes response termination
body: **Pheromone-binding protein**, or PBP, is a soluble protein in the fluid surrounding sensory endings inside an antennal sensillum. Shiota and colleagues deleted BmPBP1 and tested whether its contribution extended beyond increasing sensitivity. Antennal recordings measured the rise and recovery of responses to 200-ms odor pulses.

The knockout antennae remained responsive but produced smaller EAG peaks at the same dose. The investigators therefore compared kinetics while accounting for response amplitude. After that control, knockout responses recovered more slowly, whereas response rise and onset latency did not differ in the same way.

BmPBP1 contributes to termination of the peripheral response as well as detection sensitivity. The knockout does not reveal precisely how the protein clears receptor stimulation. Capturing or redistributing pheromone are proposed explanations; the study does not establish that BmPBP1 enzymatically destroys bombykol.

body: Shiota and colleagues tested individual bombykol-responsive neurons with single-sensillum recordings. slides.title: Slow termination changes the surge–turn sequence
body: Peripheral timing can affect the reset of searching behavior. Shiota and colleagues measured tethered males’ body angle during isolated and repeated bombykol exposure. Knockouts retained the complete surge–zigzag sequence after a single pulse, but their initial surge lasted longer than in normal males.

At 0.17 Hz, successive contacts restarted surges in both groups. At 0.83 and 2 Hz, knockouts had lower surge rates and more zigzag turning. They also produced fewer surges lasting more than 2 s during the 2-Hz train, despite the prolonged response to an isolated stimulus.

A longer sensory response does not necessarily produce more sustained forward progress under repeated stimulation. The authors proposed that poor separation of onsets prevents efficient resetting. The concordance among sensory and behavioral measurements supports this explanation without recording the intervening central circuit directly.

slides.title: Binding-protein loss delays source finding
body: Shiota and colleagues allowed males to walk freely in a wind tunnel toward pulsed bombykol or real females. Normal moths received 1–100 ng bombykol source loads; knockouts received 100–10,000 ng to compensate for lower sensitivity. Source-finding success and time were measured separately.

Both groups could locate the source, with similar success across the tested treatments. Knockouts took longer, followed shorter forward surges and accumulated more turning. Searching toward real females produced the same qualitative combination of preserved success and reduced efficiency.

The loss of BmPBP1 therefore impairs efficient navigation without abolishing odor-guided searching. Dose comparisons and female-source tests weaken a simple insufficient-dose explanation. They do not establish that the mutant lacks spatial information entirely or isolate one central neuron responsible for the delayed arrival.

slides.title: A dedicated glomerulus relays bombykol input
body: The **antennal lobe** is the first central olfactory processing region. Bombykol-sensitive ORNs terminate in its toroid, where **projection neurons**, or PNs, carry processed information toward higher brain regions. **Local interneurons** connect within the antennal lobe and influence its input–output transformation.

Fujiwara and colleagues expressed **GCaMP**, a calcium-sensitive fluorescent protein, selectively in BmOR1 neurons. Their axon terminals were localized to the toroid. Calcium signals increased with bombykol source load and remained concentration dependent during repeated 200-ms pulses delivered every 1.2 s.

Sensory-terminal signals thus retained dose dependence even when downstream PN firing became less dose dependent after repeated stimulation. The comparison locates an additional transformation within the central pathway. Calcium fluorescence is an indirect activity measure and cannot be equated numerically with the firing rate recorded from a PN.

body: **Optogenetics** uses a light-sensitive protein to control selected cells. Tabuchi and colleagues expressed **channelrhodopsin-2**, or ChR2, in Bombyx bombykol-sensitive ORNs. body: **GABA**, gamma-aminobutyric acid, is an inhibitory neurotransmitter used by many antennal-lobe local interneurons. body: Fujiwara and colleagues recorded toroid PN spikes during repeated bombykol pulses at 0.83 Hz. The first response had a peak firing frequency that increased with source load. Later responses were initially suppressed and then recovered toward a settled output level.

slides.title: Accessory lobes connect with descending pathways
body: The **lateral accessory lobes**, or LALs, are paired higher-order brain regions associated with pheromone-guided motor control. **Descending neurons**, or DNs, send axons from the brain toward the ventral nervous system and thoracic motor centers. Namiki and colleagues mapped their regional arborizations in Bombyx mori.

Fluorescent dye introduced through the neck connectives labeled descending and ascending fibers. Confocal imaging revealed dense innervation in the **posterior slope**, a posterior–ventral neuropil. LAL neurons also extended processes into that region, linking two candidate sites of sensorimotor processing.

The anatomy constrains the possible routes by which pheromone information reaches motor pathways. Backfill labels fibers by their trajectory, not by neurotransmitter or response type, and includes ascending fibers as well. Dense fluorescence therefore cannot be interpreted as a count of pheromone-specific descending neurons or direct evidence of synaptic excitation.

slides.title: Descending activity can persist after an odor pulse
body: Kanzaki, Ikeda and Shibuya recorded activity from dorsal bundles of the neck connectives while delivering brief bombykol pulses. Anatomical staining identified descending neurons associated with the LAL. These recordings tested whether the motor pathway simply copied the brief duration of peripheral stimulation.

Some units switched between high- and low-frequency states after 100-ms odor pulses. The operational criterion required at least a doubling or halving of prestimulus firing that persisted for at least 5 s after stimulation ended. The response could therefore greatly outlast the input.

This **flip-flopping activity** is a persistent state change, rather than a new odor contact lasting several seconds. It is consistent with central maintenance of a searching command. Extracellular bundle recordings do not identify every contributing cell or prove that persistent firing alone produces a particular leg movement.

slides.title: Later odor pulses can switch the persistent state
body: Kanzaki and colleagues applied successive pheromone pulses to one or both antennae while recording descending units. Some units alternated between high and low firing states rather than producing an identical transient response to every presentation. Spontaneous state changes also occurred after stimulation.

In one class, two recorded signals changed in synchrony; other recordings had an opposite relationship. The maintained activity could be interrupted or switched by a later pulse, so its duration was not determined solely by the duration of one sensory stimulus.

The findings support a state-dependent central transformation between odor contact and descending output. They do not establish a fully autonomous oscillator with a fixed period or a particular recurrent inhibitory synapse. Switching, synchrony and persistence are measured response properties; the circuitry generating them remains an explanatory hypothesis.

slides.title: Serotonin changes behavioral pheromone sensitivity
body: **Serotonin**, also called 5-hydroxytryptamine, is a neurotransmitter and neuromodulator that can change a circuit’s responsiveness. Gatellier and colleagues applied it to exposed silkmoth antennal lobes and measured male responses to increasing bombykol source loads. At 10⁻⁴ mol/L, serotonin increased behavioral sensitivity. For 5 ng bombykol, the response fraction rose from 18% in the control condition to 30% during treatment. The dose-response curve returned toward the control condition after 24 h.

The effect connects a central chemical manipulation to altered behavioral initiation. It does not imply that serotonin replaces pheromone or selectively controls one identified PN. Brain exposure and pharmacological application can affect several elements, so the cellular target and signaling pathway cannot be assigned solely from the behavioral curve.

body: Gatellier and colleagues compared serotonin applications of 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻³ mol/L. The lowest concentration did not appreciably change behavioral sensitivity, the intermediate concentration enhanced it, and the highest concentration reduced it. **High-performance liquid chromatography**, or HPLC, separated serotonin from other tissue compounds for electrochemical measurement. Brain content rose from about 0.18 pmol/brain in controls to 0.44 and 0.80 pmol/brain after the intermediate and high applications. After 24 h, content returned toward control levels.

Dose-dependent effects constrain a simple uniformly excitatory explanation.

slides.title: Daily serotonin variation accompanies sensitivity
body: Gatellier and colleagues measured brain serotonin every 4 h over a 24-h light–dark cycle and tested pheromone responsiveness at multiple times. Serotonin content peaked around noon at about 0.72 pmol/brain and declined to about 0.41 pmol/brain two hours after darkness began.

For 1 ng bombykol, behavioral responsiveness rose from 32% at 06:00 to 63% around noon, then declined to 16% at 22:00. Brain serotonin and response sensitivity therefore varied together over the tested daily schedule.

The correlation is consistent with a state-dependent serotonergic contribution but does not prove that serotonin alone generates the rhythm. Measurements under a light–dark cycle also do not establish persistence of an endogenous circadian oscillator in constant conditions. Daily modulation and the separate application experiments provide different forms of evidence.

slides.title: Sensory context changes walking speed and turning
body: Yamada and colleagues measured forward and angular velocity as a function of odor-detection frequency during virtual navigation. **Angular velocity** is the rate of change of heading, distinct from translational movement through space. Wind and optic-flow direction could be reversed independently.

With correctly aligned cues, forward velocity peaked around 0.7 Hz and turning velocity around 0.4 Hz. Reversing wind removed the same frequency-dependent forward-speed pattern and shifted the turning peak toward about 0.2 Hz. Reversing visual motion also produced unequal left- and right-turning responses.

These behavioral changes establish context-dependent control rather than a fixed response to odor frequency alone. The proposed association between higher encounter rates and proximity to a female remains an interpretation, not proof that frequency uniquely determines distance. The experiment does not identify the central neurons performing the multisensory comparison.

slides.title: Aligned sensory cues improve source-finding success
body: Yamada and colleagues compared search success, arrival time and success per unit time across combinations of odor, wind and visual input. All treatments retained odor information, allowing the contributions of other cues to be evaluated against an odor-only condition.

Correctly aligned odor, wind and visual information improved performance compared with reduced-cue conditions. Reversing wind within the full-cue preparation sharply reduced success. Visual effects were context dependent: limited effects with odor alone did not mean vision was irrelevant when all three modalities were present.

The results support multisensory control of walking odor-source search. Success within a 300-s virtual trial does not establish unrestricted navigation in a natural habitat or a complete sensory-to-motor circuit. Behavioral cue manipulations complement receptor and neuronal experiments while leaving the site and synaptic mechanism of integration unresolved.

slides.title: Tracking requires detection, timing and motor state
body: Published silkmoth experiments link several transformations: ligand-selective receptors excite a defined sensory channel; peripheral binding-protein function helps responses terminate; and antennal-lobe neurons combine or separate contacts according to input strength. These are experimentally distinguishable operations rather than one generic measure of olfactory sensitivity.

BmPBP1 loss preserves searching but reduces its temporal efficiency. Optogenetic paired inputs reveal central integration within tens of milliseconds, while descending recordings reveal states lasting seconds after brief stimulation. The different timescales permit short odor encounters to influence extended motor behavior.

No cited study establishes every synapse from bombykol binding to a completed plume-tracking trajectory. GABA pharmacology, serotonin application and anatomical overlap constrain mechanisms without resolving all receptor subtypes, intrinsic channels or causal motor assignments. Natural searching combines these sensory and central operations with wind and visual information.

items.text: Turbulence creates odor contacts and gaps; encounter timing can renew surges or permit casting rather than supplying a smooth concentration gradient.
Adding a foreign receptor to bombykol neurons changes which ligand initiates searching while preserving their central toroid targets.
Ligand-selective OR and Orco subunits support odor-gated currents; patch recordings and residue substitutions constrain the channel mechanism.
BmPBP1 loss prolongs sensory responses, blurs repeated contacts and delays source finding despite preserved searching and eventual success.
Weak contacts can integrate over tens of milliseconds; GABA limits strong-input integration, and descending signals can persist for seconds.
Serotonin alters responsiveness in a dose-dependent manner, while wind and visual feedback influence odor-guided movement and source-finding success.
